stops.name: The Tafna, the second and larger treaty
stops.campa: On the banks of the Tafna river Bugeaud himself, needing a free hand to take Constantine in the east, signs a treaty that concedes Abd al-Qadir even more than Desmichels had: the whole of Oran and Titteri provinces, two-thirds of Algeria, under his rule in fact if not in French law. The emir now governs from the Kabylie to Biskra to the Moroccan border. He will have barely two years of peace to make of this vast concession a working state before Paris decides the concession was a mistake.

stops.name: Tagdemt, Léon Roches at the emir's table
stops.campa: A young Frenchman calling himself a convert, fluent in Arabic and useful with a pen, enters the emir's household as secretary, drafting his letters to French commanders in the idiom of European diplomacy. Abd al-Qadir, whose court welcomes scholars and deserters alike and judges men by their learning and their word, trusts him with correspondence for nearly two years. Only later will it become known that the secretary reported everything to Algiers, and that trust, in this war as in every war, has a price the emir will keep paying.

stops.name: Tagdemt, the capital raised from nothing
stops.campa: On the site of an old Almoravid fortress near Tiaret the emir builds his capital: mosque, arsenal, powder mill, foundries worked by deserters from three European armies, workshops weaving the cloth for uniformed regiments, schools teaching Qur'an and arithmetic to the children of the tribes. He divides his country into eight khalifaliks under governors answerable to him, keeps a standing army of eight thousand infantry and two thousand horse, and mints his own silver coin, the muhammadiyya, so that his soldiers need not be paid in another sovereign's face. It is, briefly, the only modern Algerian state that will exist for a century.

stops.name: The Mitidja, the treaty broken
stops.campa: In October the Duke of Orléans marches an army through the mountain passage of the Iron Gates from Constantine to Algiers, a route the Tafna treaty had left to the emir's discretion; Abd al-Qadir declares the crossing an act of war. On the twentieth of November he throws his cavalry across the Mitidja plain, burning the French colonial farms up to the walls of Algiers itself, and sends a formal letter of war to the governor-general. Ten years of the harder war, the war of total conquest, begin here.

stops.name: Tagdemt, the capital destroyed
stops.campa: Bugeaud, back as governor-general with a doubled army and a new doctrine — razzia, the burning of crops and herds, war carried to the whole population rather than to armies alone — takes and levels Tagdemt. The emir has already learned not to keep a capital an enemy can seize; the state moves into the smala, an entire mobile city of tens of thousands, tents, workshops, treasury, harem, and library struck and reloaded onto camels within hours, obedient to no fixed address the French can march to.

stops.name: Taguine, the smala taken
stops.campa: Near the spring of Taguine, south of Boghar, the Duke of Aumale's flying column stumbles by chance on the emir's entire mobile capital, some thirty thousand souls camped in the belief that no French force could reach so far so fast. Abd al-Qadir himself is a day's ride away; in a few hours of chaos his treasury, his library worth by French estimate five thousand pounds sterling, three thousand of his people, and the material apparatus of eleven years of state-building are captured or scattered. He loses in an afternoon what Tagdemt took a decade to build, and never again commands a fixed home for his people.

stops.name: Across the Moulouya, refuge in Morocco
stops.campa: Stripped of his capital, the emir withdraws west across the Moulouya river into the territory of Sultan Abd al-Rahman ben Hicham of Morocco, who extends him protection and, quietly, arms and men — the two rulers bound by faith against the shared French threat. From Moroccan soil, and from the tribes still loyal on both sides of the border he no longer fully controls, Abd al-Qadir keeps the war alive for four more years, a fugitive government raiding into a country that is legally no longer his to raid.

stops.name: Isly, the Sultan's army broken for his sake
stops.campa: France, unwilling to tolerate a sanctuary across the border, bombards Tangier and Mogador and sends Bugeaud against the Moroccan army mustered at Djarf el-Akhdar near Oujda. On the Isly river the Sultan's forces, fighting in part for the emir they have sheltered, break and scatter toward the Moulouya. Abd al-Qadir has cost his host a battle and, soon, a treaty; the debt of hospitality between the two Muslim sovereigns is about to come due against him.

stops.name: Tangier, the treaty that expels him
stops.campa: Defeated at Isly, Sultan Abd al-Rahman signs at Tangier a treaty binding him to declare Abd al-Qadir an outlaw and refuse him further refuge in Morocco. The Sultan's protection does not vanish overnight — the border country remains porous, and the emir will fight from its edges for three more years — but the treaty marks the closing of the last door a sovereign state had left open to him. From here the war is fought by a man with no capital, no recognized ally, and a shrinking country of loyal tribes.

stops.name: Nekmaria, the caves of the Dahra
stops.campa: In the Dahra massif, allies of the emir's cause, the Ouled Riah, take refuge from Pélissier's column in the cave of Ghar el-Frechih near Nekmaria and refuse to come out and surrender. Pélissier orders fires lit at every mouth of the cave and keeps them burning from the eighteenth of June through the twentieth; more than a thousand men, women, and children die of the smoke inside the rock. Word of it reaches the emir's camp as it reaches every tribe in the west: proof, needing none, of what submission to the French army can cost a people who trust it, and one more reason the war his oath committed him to cannot yet be laid down.

stops.name: Sidi Brahim, the last great victory
stops.campa: Crossing back from Moroccan sanctuary, the emir's cavalry surrounds a small French column of chasseurs and infantry near the marabout of Sidi Brahim; the column fights three days from a walled farmhouse and a ravine before it is overrun, its survivors nearly all killed or captured. It becomes, on the French side, a legend of last-stand heroism taught to schoolchildren for a century; on Abd al-Qadir's side it is simply the war working as he has always meant it to work — swift cavalry striking an exposed column far from support — and the last time it will work so completely.

stops.name: The deira on the Moulouya, the prisoners' deaths
stops.campa: Three hundred miles from where the emir himself is fighting, officers of his mobile camp, fearing their own captives will be freed by an approaching French force, order some three hundred French prisoners executed on the Moulouya, sparing eleven officers. Abd al-Qadir, who has issued his own regulations for the humane treatment of prisoners and fought to be recognized as waging a lawful war between nations rather than a rebellion, will spend the rest of his life answering for an order he did not give and could not have countermanded in time — and will, in captivity, ask his own biographer to set the record straight in writing.
